title: Keyboard or Mouse Not Working
cardText: Diagnose a keyboard or mouse that does not respond, disconnects or behaves unexpectedly.
Check USB connections, batteries, wireless receivers, Bluetooth pairing and Windows drivers.
Determine whether the problem is with the device, connection or computer.
text: This guide helps troubleshoot external keyboards and mice on Windows computers.
Start with simple connection and power checks before changing Windows settings.
Identify whether the device uses a USB cable, a wireless USB receiver or Bluetooth.
If neither keyboard nor mouse works, try a known-working wired USB device before continuing.
The Windows instructions are primarily for Windows 11.

identifyAffectedDevice.title: Identify the affected device
body: Determine whether the keyboard, mouse or both devices are affected.
Check whether the computer itself is responding. Look for a frozen screen, unresponsive applications or a system that has stopped starting up.
If both input devices fail together, try another known-working wired USB keyboard or mouse.
If only one device is affected, begin by checking its connection type.

checkConnectionType.title: Identify the connection type
body: Check how the affected keyboard or mouse connects to the computer.
A wired USB device has a cable connected directly to the computer.
A wireless device may use a small USB receiver or connect through Bluetooth.
Wireless USB receivers and Bluetooth connections are different and require separate checks.

checkUsbConnection.title: Check the wired USB connection
body: Disconnect and reconnect the keyboard or mouse.
Try another USB port, preferably directly on the computer.
Avoid USB hubs and docking stations during testing.
Check the cable and connector for visible damage.
Allow Windows a moment to detect the reconnected device.
If the device now responds, the connection or original USB port may have been the problem.

checkWirelessPower.title: Check wireless device power
body: Confirm the keyboard or mouse is switched on.
Replace the batteries with fresh ones or fully recharge the device.
Check battery orientation and the battery compartment contacts where applicable.
Look for any power or connection indicator lights.
Move the device closer to the computer while testing.
If the device now works, the problem was likely related to power or range.

link.name: Microsoft: Mouse and keyboard problems
link.description: Official checks for wireless device batteries, switches and connections.

replaceBatteries.title: Replace batteries or recharge the device
body: Fit fresh batteries or recharge the keyboard or mouse.
Confirm the device switches on.
Test it again after restoring power.
If the device still does not power on, check its battery contacts, charging cable and power switch.
A device that remains completely unresponsive may require repair or replacement.

identifyWirelessConnection.title: Does the device use a USB wireless receiver?
body: Look for a small USB receiver plugged into the computer.
Some receivers are stored inside the mouse or keyboard battery compartment when not in use.
Devices using a dedicated USB receiver usually do not need Windows Bluetooth pairing.
If there is no USB receiver and the device is paired directly through Windows Bluetooth settings, choose Bluetooth.

checkWirelessReceiver.title: Check the wireless USB receiver
body: Confirm the receiver is firmly connected to a working USB port.
Unplug it, wait approximately 10 seconds and reconnect it.
Try another USB port directly on the computer.
Move the receiver closer to the wireless device if possible.
Keep the receiver away from obvious sources of wireless interference.
Some keyboards and mice require a manufacturer-specific receiver and cannot use a generic replacement.

link.name: Microsoft: Wireless mouse and keyboard troubleshooting
link.description: Official instructions for checking USB wireless receivers and connections.

checkReceiverPairing.title: Check receiver compatibility and pairing
body: Confirm the USB receiver belongs to the affected keyboard or mouse.
Some manufacturers provide software for pairing a compatible replacement receiver.
Check whether the device has a connection or pairing button.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions for that exact model.
Do not attempt Windows Bluetooth pairing for a device that only supports a dedicated USB receiver.
If the receiver or device still fails, test with another computer where practical.

checkBluetoothConnection.title: Check the Bluetooth connection
body: Open Settings, Bluetooth & devices.
Confirm Bluetooth is switched on.
Check whether the keyboard or mouse appears in the connected devices list.
Move the device closer to the computer and confirm its battery is charged.
If Bluetooth is missing from Windows settings, the computer may have a Bluetooth adapter or driver problem.
If the device is not connected, try pairing it again.

repairBluetooth.title: Reconnect or pair the Bluetooth device
body: Ensure the keyboard or mouse is switched on and charged.
Open Windows Settings, Bluetooth & devices.
If the device is already listed but will not connect, remove it from the list.
Put the device into pairing mode using the manufacturer's instructions.
Select Add device, then Bluetooth, and choose the keyboard or mouse.
Follow any pairing prompts, including entering a code on a Bluetooth keyboard if requested.
If pairing fails, try switching Bluetooth off and on, then repeat.

testAlternateInput.title: Test a known-working keyboard or mouse
body: Connect a known-working wired USB keyboard or mouse directly to the computer.
If both original devices were affected, test at least one replacement of each type where possible.
Try a different USB port if the replacement does not respond.
If the replacement works, investigate the original device, receiver or connection.
If the replacement also fails, investigate the computer and USB ports.

deviceFault.title: Original device or connection fault likely
body: A known-working replacement device responds normally.
This suggests a problem with the original keyboard, mouse, cable, wireless receiver or pairing.
If possible, test the original device on another compatible computer.
Check for a damaged cable, faulty batteries or a missing receiver.
Repair or replace the faulty device if necessary.

checkUsbPorts.title: Check the computer's USB ports
body: Test a known-working USB device in more than one port.
For a desktop computer, try a rear motherboard USB port instead of a front-panel port.
Disconnect unnecessary USB hubs and docking stations.
Check whether the ports work before Windows starts, such as in the BIOS or UEFI setup, if you are comfortable accessing it.
Do not change BIOS or UEFI settings unnecessarily.
If several ports fail with known-working devices, the problem may involve USB hardware or the operating system.

usbPortFault.title: USB port or controller problem
body: Known-working USB devices are not responding through the computer's USB ports.
Try ports on a different USB controller if available.
If the ports work in BIOS or UEFI but not Windows, investigate Windows USB drivers and recent changes.
If the ports also fail before Windows starts, a hardware problem is more likely.
Check for physical damage and arrange further diagnostics if necessary.

checkDeviceManager.title: Check the keyboard and mouse in Device Manager
body: Right-click Start and open Device Manager, using a working input device.
Expand Keyboards and Mice and other pointing devices.
For wireless devices, also check Bluetooth and Human Interface Devices where appropriate.
Look for warning symbols, disabled devices or missing hardware.
Open the affected device's Properties and review Device status for an error code.
If there is no obvious driver error, continue with additional troubleshooting.

link.name: Microsoft: Mouse and keyboard driver troubleshooting
link.description: Official instructions for checking and updating input device drivers.

reinstallDrivers.title: Update or reinstall the affected driver
body: Before making changes, ensure you have another working input method available.
In Device Manager, right-click the affected keyboard, mouse or Bluetooth adapter.
Try Update driver and follow the instructions.
Check the computer or device manufacturer's support website for a compatible driver if needed.
If updating does not help, uninstall the affected device and restart Windows to allow it to be detected again.
Avoid removing unrelated HID devices or multiple input drivers at once.
Retest the keyboard or mouse after restarting.

link.name: Microsoft: Mouse and keyboard problems
link.description: Official Windows guidance for input device connections and drivers.

link.name: Microsoft: Update Bluetooth drivers
link.description: Instructions for updating, reinstalling or rolling back a Bluetooth adapter driver.

checkSafeMode.title: Test the device in Windows Safe Mode
body: If you have a working keyboard or mouse, restart Windows into Safe Mode.
Safe Mode starts Windows with a limited set of drivers and services.
Test a wired USB keyboard or mouse where possible because some wireless or Bluetooth features may not operate in Safe Mode.
If the device works in Safe Mode but fails during normal Windows startup, a software or driver conflict is possible.
If the device still fails, further testing is required to distinguish software from hardware.
Restart Windows normally after the test.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows startup settings and Safe Mode
link.description: Official instructions for entering and exiting Windows Safe Mode.

softwareConflict.title: Software or driver conflict likely
body: The device works in Safe Mode but not during normal Windows operation.
Check whether the problem started after installing an application, driver or Windows update.
Investigate keyboard and mouse utilities, device management software and startup applications.
Update or roll back a recently changed driver where appropriate.
Test again during normal Windows startup after making one change at a time.

hardwareEscalation.title: Further input device diagnostics required
body: The keyboard or mouse is still not working after connection, power, driver and operating system checks.
Test the original device on another computer if possible.
If multiple known-working USB devices fail on the same computer, investigate USB controllers, motherboard connections or Windows installation problems.
If only one wireless device fails, investigate its receiver, radio connection or hardware.
Record any Device Manager error codes and troubleshooting results before arranging repair or further diagnostics.
